decidedValue.signpostBody: The course has six short lessons, each built around a situation you might actually face. First, a weak result and the choice between honest reporting and a stronger impression. Second, correcting an unsupported claim in shared work. Third, a fairness issue in shared work. Fourth, raising an unacknowledged contribution. Fifth, weighing your own habits against a profession's expectations. Sixth, acting on a new ethical responsibility without being asked. Work through them in order; each builds on the one before.
decidedValue.signpostInstruction: Work through the six lessons in order.
decidedValue.overview:
This course assumes you can already reference accurately and consistently, and that you already understand why academic work does so. What it adds is judgement under pressure: the ethical choices that referencing and attribution raise once you are working independently, in shared work, or in a professional role where getting it wrong has consequences beyond a lost mark.

By the end you will be able to justify your own course of action when a weak result tempts you toward a stronger impression than the evidence supports, act to correct an unsupported claim in shared work, respond to a fairness issue around an unacknowledged contribution, critique your own habits against a profession's ethical expectations, and recognise and act on a new ethical responsibility without being asked.
decidedValue.courseOutcomesFraming: Six flat learning outcomes, read from crs-07_tiered-outcomes (pathway-distillation profile: crs-03 is not-applicable), framed up front: justifying honest reporting over a stronger impression, correcting an unsupported claim, responding to a fairness issue, raising an unacknowledged contribution, critiquing one's own habits against professional ethical expectations, and acting unprompted on a new ethical responsibility.

practiceConnection.academic: These are not abstract ethical puzzles: they are the situations that come up in a dissertation, a group project, a placement or a first professional role, where a weak result, an unattributed contribution, or an unfamiliar source type lands on your desk with no one checking your working. The judgement this course builds sits alongside your critical and research practice, informing the same honesty that underpins every claim you make and every source you cite elsewhere.

decidedValue.summary: You have reached the end of the course, and of this pathway. Referencing is no longer a mechanical or even a judgement skill: it is an ethical practice you can be trusted with. You can justify your own course of action when a weak result tempts you toward a stronger impression, act to correct an unsupported claim in shared work, respond to a fairness issue around an unacknowledged contribution, critique your own habits against a profession's ethical expectations, and recognise and act on a new ethical responsibility without being asked. Look back at the confidence check to see how far this has moved, and carry this judgement into whatever comes next in your own academic and professional practice.

practiceConnection.academic: From here, this is a habit you carry rather than a course you finish. Notice the moment a weak result tempts you toward a stronger impression, and choose honest reporting anyway. Notice an unsupported claim or an unacknowledged contribution in shared work, and act on it even when the conversation is uncomfortable. This same ethical attention underpins the arguments you build in your academic writing, the rigour you bring to researching and investigating, and the judgement you exercise whenever you read and evaluate critically: it is not a separate strand of your practice but the integrity running through all of them.

items.stem: Your results are weaker than expected. Reporting them honestly risks a less impressive outcome than quietly rounding the figures favourably. What justifies the honest choice?
You notice an unsupported figure in a piece of shared work that no one else has spotted. What justifies correcting it rather than leaving it?
Raising a fairness issue in shared work means an uncomfortable conversation with people you work closely with. What justifies speaking up anyway?
A contribution to shared work has gone unacknowledged. What does raising it with those involved, respectfully, aim to achieve?
You compare your own habits of honesty and attribution against a profession's ethical expectations. What should that critique help you identify?
In a new professional role, you notice an ethical responsibility that no one has asked you to take on. What does acting on it, and explaining it to someone newer, demonstrate?
